clinicalPearls: Presents as a greenish to blue-green discolouration of one or more nails, most often a single fingernail or toenail, caused by colonisation with Pseudomonas aeruginosa producing the pigments pyocyanin and pyoverdine.
Almost always develops on a background of pre-existing onycholysis or chronic paronychia, where the detached nail plate creates a moist subungual space favouring bacterial growth.
Prolonged immersion in water is the dominant risk factor, so it is common in cleaners, dishwashers, bar staff, healthcare workers and swimmers.
The classic triad is green discolouration, proximal chronic paronychia and distolateral onycholysis; the pigment lies within the nail plate rather than beneath it.
Wood's light examination may show green fluorescence, and gently trimming or clipping the detached nail confirms the pigment is on the undersurface of the plate.

Management centres on keeping the nail dry, clipping away the onycholytic portion and treating with topical antiseptic or dilute acetic acid soaks; systemic therapy is rarely required in the immunocompetent.
Although a Pseudomonas colonisation, it is classified as a non-infective nail dyschromia because it reflects surface colonisation of an already-damaged nail rather than an invasive tissue infection.
Recurrence is common if the underlying onycholysis or wet-work exposure is not addressed.
reference.pathophysiology: The discolouration arises when Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonises the space created by onycholysis or chronic paronychia. The organism thrives in the warm, moist microenvironment beneath a detached nail plate and elaborates water-soluble pigments, chiefly the blue-green pyocyanin and the yellow-green fluorescent pyoverdine (fluorescein). These diffuse into the ventral nail plate and impart the characteristic green to blue-black hue. There is no true invasion of the nail matrix or bed in the immunocompetent host; the process is essentially a superficial colonisation of already-diseased keratin, which is why it responds to drying measures and removal of the affected plate rather than requiring aggressive systemic antimicrobials.
additionalDifferentials: Nail plate melanonychia or subungual melanoma
Chromogenic mould or fungal onychomycosis (e.g. Aspergillus, Scytalidium)
Exogenous staining from dyes, tobacco or topical agents
additionalInvestigations: Clinical and Wood's light examination for green fluorescence
Bacterial culture of subungual debris or nail clipping
Nail clipping for mycology to exclude concurrent onychomycosis
Dermoscopy of the nail plate to assess pigment distribution
Assessment of the affected nail for underlying onycholysis or paronychia
Consideration of occupational and wet-work history
redFlags: Green discolouration accompanied by spreading erythema, pain, fever or lymphangitis suggesting invasive soft-tissue infection
Onset in an immunocompromised or diabetic patient where systemic Pseudomonas infection is a risk
Failure to resolve with drying measures, prompting reconsideration of melanoma or chromogenic fungal infection
A single darkening streak or Hutchinson sign that raises concern for subungual melanoma
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, with most cases resolving once the nail is kept dry and the onycholytic portion is removed. Recurrence is frequent when the underlying onycholysis, paronychia or wet-work exposure persists.
pitfalls: Mistaking the green pigment for a subungual haematoma or melanoma and either over-investigating or under-investigating
Treating with topical or oral antifungals on the assumption of onychomycosis without recognising the bacterial cause
Failing to address the underlying onycholysis or moisture exposure, leading to relapse
Assuming systemic antibiotics are needed in an otherwise well patient when local measures suffice
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management, current edition
management: Clip away the detached onycholytic portion of the nail plate to eliminate the moist subungual space that Pseudomonas colonises
Apply topical antiseptics such as dilute acetic acid soaks or sodium hypochlorite, or a topical antipseudomonal agent (fluoroquinolone or aminoglycoside drops), to the exposed nail bed
Keep the nail dry and treat the underlying onycholysis or chronic paronychia that predisposes to recolonisation
Advise avoidance of prolonged water immersion and wearing of protective gloves for wet work
Reserve systemic antipseudomonal therapy with an oral fluoroquinolone for extensive, refractory or immunocompromised cases
Exclude and treat any coexisting onychomycosis that perpetuates the onycholysis
